projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Edward Roll was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II Veteran Edward W. Roll. Mr. Roll served in the U.S. Army in the 156th Regiment. Edward's highest rank was Sergeant and he served in the European theater. I'm Tom Swope and this recording was made at my home in Mentor, Ohio, on June 5th, 2003. Edward was 82 at the time of this recording.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah, I'm sure I've been by it. I'm sure.

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you have specific memories of December 7th, 1941?

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: Oh, yes. Uh-huh. We were just, I guess, listening to the radio and or afterward.... Was I in church, maybe; came home from church and heard the announcement?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Probably when you came home from --

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: Was it Sunday?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -- church. It was Sunday and I think --

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -- they got the word in the afternoon at this point.

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: That's... We were holy and we went to church. I had brothers and sisters that we would go to church and come home and play the polka on the -- on the radio. I mean, on the records. And I think that's when it happened. That's when we had a little radio then. So, we remembered pretty good.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What did you think when you heard that news?

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: I don't remember what I was thinking. I'm sorry.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How old were you?

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: Well, I was born in 1920; so, that's 1941.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you --

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: Twenty-one years. Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So, you were probably working at that time?

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: Yes. Yes, I was working. And --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What kind of job did you have then?

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: I was working in a factory and worked for Lincoln Electric on the east side. I lived in Brooklyn, took the streetcar to downtown. Took the downtown streetcar all the way to work. It was nice.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did that job give you draft deferments?

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: No. No, draft deferments.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So when were you called?

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: And we didn't get credit for the service toward our pension. It was strict company.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh (affirmative).

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So, the time you were --

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: But that's all right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -- in the military it didn't count? Did you say --

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: Didn't count for the service toward the pension.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: For the pension.

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: Counted service for the company, but not for the pension.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Ah. I see.

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: Yeah. You had to be there and earn your keep. Yeah. So.... Then the... Okay. I was going to enlist in the Navy with a buddy of mine, but he didn't pass the physical; so, I forgot about it until I got drafted in May of 1943 and left Cleveland the 20th of May and went up to Camp Perry. Stayed there for a couple of days and got boots and shoes and clothes and stuff. And, then, we took a nice train ride all the way from Ohio down to Camp Shelby, Mississippi. Got down there it was nice and warm. Really warm. And we did -- I did basic training, three months, boot camp, in the 69th Infantry Division in Camp Shelby, Mississippi.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was it tough for you to be thrown into a situation with guys from all over the country when you went into training?

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: No, not really. It was... It was a new experience for me. We had, you know, Southerners and... I adapted real well, I think. I'm pretty sure.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Any interesting stories from your training that you could tell me?

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: Oh, well, it was kind of rough. We had hikes, full fill pack hikes. We'd go out in the -- and camp in tents and on the rifle range, you know. And my sister came down once to see me. She had a boyfriend also near Camp Shelby. But, otherwise, it was a nice experience. I enjoyed it, really. Saturday, why, we'd -- afternoon, why, we'd go to the, you know, PX and we'd go to the town once in a while, Biloxi. No. What is it? Camp Shelby... What's the town there?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Well, I think my --

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: I got a blank on it. I know the name of that town.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: But I think my dad spent some time at Camp Shelby. I can't remember the town, though.

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: Oh. Were you in the service?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: No. My father was in the military.

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So, that was about three months you --

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: Yeah. Three months. I came home, then, on -- after three months basic training and had two weeks at home. You know. Had a nice time at home with family and had a girlfriend then and... So, then, after we went back to Camp Shelby and shortly after we got shipped out. Another train ride all the way up to New York near the port of embarkation. And over there we got our dental work and all our shots and stuff and our new clothing and duffle bag and all that stuff. And had a nice time over there with a friend from back east. Still lives at Serly(phonetic), Serling(phonetic), Ohio? Eddy Maybaugh(phonetic). And he owns a furniture store there. I'm going to have to go and see him. I have talked to him in the past. And he was a Sergeant. And he was familiar with New York because he would go as a buyer if he could buy for his furniture store in New York. So, he took me to a nice small Italian restaurant in -- I forget what the name of it was, but it was close to downtown. Then, after that, we went to Radio City. Saw the show. So, after that, well, we got ready to leave and we left at, oh, it was early in the morning; 3:00 o'clock in the morning, I guess, they had us lined up on the docks, you know. And, then, we boarded the Queen Elizabeth. And this was the original Queen Elizabeth. I don't know; I think there was another one since.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah, right.

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: Yeah, there's another one now. So, then, we went, found our bunks and sacked out for a little while. We got up in the morning we were on our way. And the weather outside, of course, being in New York, it was November, it was chilly, you know. And after we got up in the morning, why, we were -- the boat was on its way and the air was kind of warm. And, here, they went down the coast of the United States down to Florida and, then, went across the ocean towards Africa and, then, back up. And we traveled alone. The boat traveled alone, zig-zagging all the way across to avoid the subs. We were glad of that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So there were no sub scares on that --

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -- crossing?

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: There was no sub scares. No. And, then, after four days we landed in Greenock, Scotland. And it was really interesting, that boat ride. When you got up to Ireland they had the Irish swells. Did you ever hear of them?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: Well, the boat -- this is a large boat and the boat was rocking gently all the way. Called Irish swells.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Lot of seasickness?

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: No, not then. So, we got off in Greenock, Scotland, and they had -- the boat couldn't go up to the dock, but it left us off in small boats and when we got to the dock, why, there was these old English trains, you know, where you get in on the outside.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: So, everybody piled into there. We didn't -- they didn't monkey around with us. They just... Then took us down into Central England, Manchester. It was a big English military center. And we were stationed there for a while. And, then, oh, we were just sitting around, sitting around, sitting around. Everybody once... You know, once in a while everybody would get pulled out and sent to this different unit. So, I got transferred over to the 156 Infantry Regiment as a Medic. Had to go through training again as a Medic. So, that was okay. They shipped us over to place called Ilfracombe. It's... I don't know if you're familiar with the English map. You got Cornwall coming down. And, then, there's a big bay and, then, up on the other side of the bay was Wales. And we were on the other side. Ilfracombe.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So, you were on the east or west side of England?

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: We were on the north side of this Land's End or Cornwall, I think it's called. We were on the north end.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I'd have to look at a map.

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: And this place, Ilfracombe, was a summer resort. And they had a real big huge beach. It was... 'Course, it was wintertime, it was deserted; but, the Army had taken it over and they used it for tank landing practices. So, we would be the Medics attached to this 156 Infantry Regiment. It was a separate regiment. It used to be Louisiana National Guard. And years ago they had four regiments to a division in the Army. Then they streamlined it to three divisions. So, this 156 Infantry Regiment was alone. And it was mainly guard duties. All kind of rear action duties. One battalion, one company was up in Scotland guarding the submarine bases up there and a second battalion was guarding sheep. (Interruption)

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: All right. So, where were we?

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: So, second battalion's guarding sheep. Eisenhower's headquarters in London. And it was all, like, military police duty also. They were kind of scattered all over. I'd be with a bunch of buddies and, then, all of a sudden they would take a few to -- for going to one duty and this and that. So, then, okay, after... Let's see. We stayed there in the wintertime, over the winter of '43-'44. Had a nice... English were nice. You know. We had -- they had a nice dance hall down in town and we'd get invited out for a Christmas or a Thanksgiving dinner. Well, it was beyond Thanksgiving.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: Christmas, you know. And we were treated real nice. We had a good time there. Then in the spring we were shipped down to Lands End down in Cornwall. They had a big area to where all the troops were being gathered. And this was before D- Day. So, we stayed there and did basically nothing, really. Waiting, waiting, waiting. Then, finally, of course, the D- Day came along and we were still there. So, we stayed in England until three months after D-day. Then we were shipped out of Southampton across to Normandy. And we didn't see any action there. Everything was over with already, you know. So, we... Let's see. We went -- stayed around Cherbourg for a little bit. And, then, they put us in truck and took us around the countryside. We went to the western part of France, Brest. Then, finally, they shipped us all the way to Paris. And we settled in a suburb of Paris called St. Clue(phonetic). Did you ever hear of that? No?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I think I may have.

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: It's spelled Cloud. English.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Sure. Okay.

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: St. Cloud.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: But St. Clue(phonetic). French.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: And it was up on a hill up outside of Paris and you could see the whole town of Paris, you know. So, we stayed there for a while and basically didn't have too much to do either. We'd go into the dances in the... Saturday night. You'd go walk down a hill there. Had a dance floor there. And one interesting thing about that was they had, of course, French civilians in there, too. And we were in __ we were intruders, really. And all of a sudden there's a big commotion and a crowd of people in there. Out of the crowd bust, burst two women that were bald-headed. And they had been collaborators with the Nazis. And they had wanted to -- still wanted to be part of the crowd; they had wigs on, you know. So, they were -- they discovered, the French discovered them and they beat on them a little bit. So....

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were the French people nice to you guys, to the Americans?

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: Yeah. We got along pretty good. In fact, we met two sisters in this one suburb and one had gone to the United States Miami University. She was real -- could speak real English. And her sister also could speak English and they invited us out to their house on a Sunday for cookies and cocoa and they were real nice. Basically we got along with the French. Yeah. Maybe they didn't think us were too nice. Sometimes we would get liquored up a little bit, you know. Be kind of rude. But.... So, then, we stayed there till the Battle of the Bulge broke out. And, then, what happened there, they took a third of our outfit and shipped them to the Battle of the Bulge toward Germany. And the rest of us they shipped all the way back to Normandy, because they had these twenty thousand German troops on the Isle of Geurnsey. And they thought, well, if the Battle of the Bulge, if the Germans broke through, why, they would release these prisoners on the Island. They had several small boats. They would pull nuisance raids. And that's what's part of that in that story there. And we were stationed in Carteret, a small fishing village down... Oh, the coast of Normandy, Normandy comes around this like this and goes over to this. You got a corner there. It was up above the corner. North of Mont Saint Michel. And we didn't have too much to do there. But our Captain was a doctor, Captain Ettson(phonetic). He was from the hills of -- he was from New Jersey -- New Hampshire. He loved to take us out for hikes. Okay; fall out. And we were stationed at this one time on a -- oh, in England we were stationed at a castle, at a large castle. They had Quonset huts set up for us. And he had real large estate and he had deer running around this place. And he'd take us for a hike down there. This is back in England. I'm getting backwards again.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's all right.

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: So, coming back, we wound up back in Normandy in this Careret. It was a big double house and we had to set up a dispensary upstairs. Paint the walls first, you guys. They would... Captain would get paint for us and we would go and set up a four-bed dispensary. A sick bay. And I was on duty one night and downstairs they had a, like, a room, rec room. And they -- we had to heat the water on the stove of one of these potbelly stoves, the old fashioned Army stove. And somebody closed the lid on the water. I came bouncing downstairs. I had fed the people in Sick Bay. Was going to get some water to wash the utensils, you know. And I lifted up the lid. Whew. I got a face full of steam. And it hit me and it kind of put me into shock. And I wasn't able to function my duty anymore that night. In fact, I went back to bed. We had cots up on the third floor for our beds. Stretchers, really. And Captain came then and looked at my eyes. He says, well, at least you didn't get your eyes. But I got like a three degree, third degree burn and it peeled on me like a sunburn.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: I was out for, you know, I was out of it for about a couple days. And then I got over it okay. I was just telling some of that. I never got a Purple Heart for that. Well, anyway, this raid came along and it was further up north, why, they would come and they wanted it to do sabotage work, you know. It describes it a little bit in there. And we got into the tail end of it, in a way. One night that we went out and we captured six or -- at least three, three Germans. One had been shot in the chest and one was just wounded. So, we had a tent set up, you know, and... And the aid that they gave them didn't seem to help much, but it was first aid stuff. Then the Navy came early in the morning and they took these people away. I guess the one prisoner had died then.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How far off the coast was Geurnsey?

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: Just about twenty miles, I guess.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And it was in the Channel; right?

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: Yeah. Well, I think it was outside of the Channel, Really.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Like south or whatever or --

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: Probably...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -- (unintelligible) or wester(sic).

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: Well, let's see. Let's see. Cherbourg's down here. This is there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Almost out into the ocean a little bit.

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: Yeah, it was a little bit out in the ocean. And they didn't -- like I said, they only had a few small boats. And they would come over, pull nuisance raids along in this. They failed one time and, then, they went -- came back that last time that we got involved with it, our men. So, while we were down there, why, I was able to go - - I had to fill a request from a friend of the family. Their son was killed in someplace in France or Germany. He was buried in the cemetery in Normandy. So, I was able to get a jeep and a driver and went up and took pictures of this and sent it home. There was quite a few graves there at that time. And, then, one other time, for recreation, we went to the Mont Saint Michel. Did you ever hear of that? And that is right in the corner, like I said, of Normandy and Brittany. And, oh, it's so old, you know, and you got a causeway going out there when the tide is in. And when the tide is out, you can't see any water. And they say don't go out and walk on the -- out toward the beach, because when the tide comes in, it'll come in so fast that you can't get back in time.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: Yeah. So, then we stayed there until spring of '44?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That would be '45, probably.

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: Oh, let's see. '43, '44 we were in England. '46. Must be --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Maybe in spring of '46? Was it after the war? You stayed there till after the war or --

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, the war was still going on.

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: Well, then they shipped us back to Le Mans.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: And piled us into 40&8s. That was fun. And we arrived in La Mans and stayed there for the rest of the duration. And they had the military DTC camp. Detention Camp for American soldiers. And all they did was -- the Drill Sergeant drilled them all day long. So, we were in charge of that. And we were billeted right in town also there. Yeah, we stayed there until... Well, then, the war was over, of course in, what was it; '45?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh (affirmative).

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: Yeah. August of '45?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's when the Pacific War ended. The European War ended in May.

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: Yeah, okay. And, then, the Jap, Japanese War...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The Japanese were bombed in August.

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: August. So, that ended in -- several months later.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh (affirmative). I think September. How did you get your Bronze Star?

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: Just for being over there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: They awarded it to --

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -- the unit or to....

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: We were -- that was the Northern France Star. And, well, let's see, like I said, we'd had -- didn't have much to do. Well, they had a nice Red Cross club in town. We'd go to dancing there. And they had a nice band from the detention center. It was a big nice brass band. Dancing, you know. We had a lot of fun. And one of their songs was -- their theme song, Get Up Those Stairs, Mademoiselle, Get Up Those Stairs, Mademoiselle, Get Up Those Stairs; We Got To Depart To The DTC. It was quite a place. That's on the grounds where the race there's held now.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right. Uh-huh (affirmative).

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: Yeah. Oh, we celebrated the French Fourth of July over there. What do they call that? Bastille Day.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Bastille Day. Sure.

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: Bastille Day. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you celebrate -- do you remember celebrating VE-Day in May?

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: Yes. Well, we didn't have too much celebration. We were, like, in a small, small towns.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: There's no large contingent of troops around. Oh, also, our outfit was guarding the Red Ball Highway. And that was a -- trucks carry supplies all the way to the line to the -- follow the troops going to the front line, American troops, and following, oh, what's that gentleman's name? General Patton.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right. The Flying Patton.

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: Flying Patton. Yeah, so, then we... Oh. Well, since we had nothing to do, why my commander says, well, Ed, Sergeant __ I was Sergeant by that time -- take a truck and a driver and go up to Brussels and get a load of books and open up a library in town for the troops. So, that's what we did. And we had a building up in the second floor. That was the library. So, then, this was in the fall of '45. And, then, oh, let's see. We'd... Like I said, not much to do. We had our ration of beer to take care of.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How much did you get?

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: Well, every time the truck went into town, they came back with a small keg of beer, you know. At one time I think we had got at least ten kegs of beer. Every night, why, we would drink a few beers and sing a few songs. And, then, one time the -- we were feeling pretty good and this guy says, oh, I know where we can get some hamburgers. So, I said okay and we all chipped in and away they went. They came back and they... Everybody tasted them and they didn't like them. I don't know what they were made of, but, they weren't very tasty like American hamburgers.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Maybe not beef.

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: Oh, they sell horse meat over in France.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: Yeah, a lot of horse meat. The butcher shops have horse heads on the front of the store.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: That's where you know how -- how you can buy horse meat there. But, no, the French people were real nice. They would... We had one small town that we went through and they made us a breakfast of eggs, you know. Of course, eggs were scarce then, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: So, we stayed in Le Mans, then, until... When was that? It was after Christmas. Oh, for... Let's see, the other Christmas before that when we were still in Normandy we went to a French church service. It was in a little -- in the country there. A few... About a mile or so away. So, my buddies and I said, well, let's go to church. It was a -- less a -- not as familiar as our churches, you know. Not as joyous, I guess. But it was a nice service. And then we got shipped out from Le Mans. It was after the year. I can't remember the Christmas there so much. Hmmm... Well, anyway, we got shipped up to Brussels and we were waiting for -- to come home. And we were in tents over there on the -- I guess it must have been a beach at one time or something. And, then, finally, we got orders to ship out. And coming back was a disappointing boat ride, because we were on a Victory ship. It was smaller than the Queen Elizabeth. But, anyway, that's where the homesickness came in.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Seasickness. Right. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: Well, one fellow, Art Calacheeko(phonetic) -- I still correspond with him and actually have seen him in Cape Cod and the other buddy is Charlie, Charlie Valcorte(phonetic). He's a Frenchman and Art was Italian. And they were good buddies from Boston; so, they both live down in Cape Cod now. And, like I said, I went to visit them a couple years ago. Had a nice time. And Art's the one that got sick. I guess the first day we got out in the Channel and that's where it was a little bit rough. And he went down to Sick Bay and he stayed there the whole trip home. So, we always kid him about that. The Channel was still __ you could see the mines in the ship -- lines for the ships, you know. But they steered clear of those.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: So, we came home and landed in New York. New Jersey. And the first meal we had was a nice big steak. So, that was okay. And, then, I -- we separated and I rode over to Camp Attebury, Indiana, where I was discharged in March of '46. But, talking about the Army food, the first meal I had in the Army was at Camp Perry it was Mutton. It, oh, boy. I couldn't eat it. And the last meal I had at Camp Attebury they tried to give me mutton. I couldn't eat that either. So, those things stick in my mind. It's silly. Yeah, so....

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have any close buddies over there?

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: In... Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Overseas?

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: Yeah, that's where these buddies were from.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: These guys were all close buddies.

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: I was a Sergeant; they were the Privates.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were you a Medic the whole time, then?

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: Yes. I got --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You didn't have to deal with many combat injuries?

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: Oh, we had some, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You did; you did have a few. Uh-huh (affirmative).

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: Yeah. And Carteret, when we were back in Normandy, shipped back in Normandy, they -- we had a anti-tank company that we were attached to. And they were just, like I said, didn't have much to do. And their Captain says, well, let's go out on -- we'll go out on the beach a ways and we'll head in and set up some steel oil drums and have some target practice. Well, lo and behold, they went into a mine field. And setting up the drums, they set off a Bouncing Betty and that, you know, that races up and explodes. And it caught two of the guys; one pretty bad, the other one not so bad. And they hadn't taken any medics with; so, they came back to town and got us and we rushed out there. And they had pulled a large size truck open, open truck in there with the drums that they had just taken off. And the truck was still sitting there. And we carefully went in on the tracks that the truck had made with our stretchers and got the two people out. Like I said, the one was unconscious and bleeding profusely. The other one was not so bad. So, we took those guys out and put them on the vehicle to take them back to town. And the truck driver says I'm going to go back in and get my truck. So, he walks back in on the same tracks. He gets in the truck, he starts it up and he backs up a few feet. He sets off a tank mine. Oh. And that took that truck and blew off one of the wheels and took that truck and set it up ninety degrees, back down again on its wheels. The driver was just sitting there like this. I thought, oh, my gosh, we got to go in and get that guy, too? He sat there for about thirty seconds. He finally got up. He had been stunned. He got up and walked out. So, we took these two casualties into town and the one I said that was hurt pretty bad, he was unconscious, bleeding profusely, and, so, they tried to give him some medica- -- they don't have blood plasma, but they had... What was it? Plasma? What they call? Anyway, it was a liquid that they had given him. I don't think it was a, like, a blood....

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Not a blood transfusion, but --

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: Oh, a blood transfusion.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -- (unintelligible) plasma.

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: I think it was plasma, yeah. And it just came right out of him. You know, they... He died. So, with the other fellow they came and -- Navy came and got him, took him to the hospital. He had superficial wounds in the back. So, that was the most harrowing experience we had. And another time we saw some cows that had been - - walked into the mine field, you know. We were curious about it. But these cattle had got killed by the mines. So, we thought we better not go in there. Didn't monkey around, you know. So, that was our close experience. Close enough, I think.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah. So, did you lose any buddies over there?

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Yeah. Right. Okay. We lost a Medic. And, again, with the -- being over in Careret, then, they had these German-built pill boxes still there, you know. And the troops were still out on the island. So, they, they had watch details that would go up to these pill boxes and just observe. Radio back if there was -- they saw something, saw somebody coming. Anyway, the Chief would go with the food up the roadway and this roadway is up on a ridge and they used to get fired at from the high on... It was so -- they could see them so clearly. Well, anyway, I was up there two -- a stretch for several days. Then another fellow, was his turn to go up. And the jeep went up for the food and change of clothing. And everybody came out to get their stuff. Just then a shell exploded overhead and killed this Medic. I forget his name. Can't think of it. That was a close one. I think that was the only one that got hurt and killed. Yeah. So... While I was over in Le Mans I got to visit a cousin of mine. He was over in the wine country of France. So, they had nice, nice electric trains in France. They still have, you know, have good... I took the train from Le Mans to Paris. And, then, went over to this -- I forget the name of the town where I visited with my cousin for a few days. And, then, another time I got -- I got to go to Switzerland on leave. I had never gone to London or anything, you know, all along the way. And the Captain said, well, why don't you go to Switzerland. So, it was a week journey and I took up with a fellow from Elyria. And he could play the piano. So, when we got to Switzerland we stayed in three different cities and three different hotels and every place that had a piano this fellow would... I forget his name, too. He would play the piano. So, it was a nice vacation in Switzerland. I bought a unique Swiss watch. I still have it at home. It has a face on top and a face down on the bottom on the same watch, you know. And the thing of it is it went on the bum at home. And my wife and I went to Europe in 1970. I took this watch with me. I was going to have it fixed in Switzerland. They wouldn't fix it for me. Said, no, we can't fix it. I brought it back home and a guy with a tool room that was dabbling with watches he fixed it for me. Well, anyway, we had a nice vacation in Switzerland, three cities. And nice train rides. And this hotel that -- well, one hotel we stayed in that I said had the piano downstairs, that fellow that played the piano, well, when my wife and I went back to Europe, we went to England, France, Switzerland, and we stayed in the same hotel where this piano was.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was there much souvenir collecting in your outfit?

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: No. Oh, just... Let's see, we went -- when we went to Brest, they had a warehouse that the Nazis had. We had small trinkets and stuff. Insignias, you know; Nazi insignias. One Nazi insignia that, like I said, back in St. Cloud in the -- we were in this suburb of Paris. You stood up on top floor, they had an open porch. Looked down on the courtyard and Germans had put their swastika in stones in the driveway, in the center of the driveway around. Oh, we had German -- in Le Mans we had German prisoners. A barber. And then we had a little bar. We had a German bartender. So, maybe he was nipping a little bit. And we had a sixteen-year-old boy that would clean up the barber shop. And he was scared. Yeah. Oh, over in England when I was attached to -- before going overseas, over to France, we were assigned to a hospital, military hospital in England that had German prisoners that were the first ones from the battle -- from the invasion.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: D-Day; right.

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: And they had limbs, you know, removed and... And this one ward they had these German ones, German soldiers. And they had a Russian. He was a shoemaker from there. And they would scare him. They said the Americans are going to kill you. And he was terribly afraid. And I remember helping the nurse change the bandages, you know. And this one fellow had his leg amputated and he had a bandage on. And I was behind her helping her and she took the bandage off and here there was -- Germans had __ doctors had put maggots in there to clean the wound. And she was frightened. She said ahhhhhh. She screamed. Run and get the can of ether spray. She had to kill them, kill the maggots. That was fun. And we did see the buzz bombs over in England while we were standing in line in this hospital unit. You could hear the thing and all of a sudden it stopped, motor would stop, boom, you would hear it. And we did see one one time. They had a break in the clouds. And you'd hear put, put, put, put, and here the thing went through the opening in the cloud. And, then, they floated somewhere, too. Yeah. Those were the good old days, huh?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yea, but none of those buzz bomb got too close, then.

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: No, they never got too close. We didn't -- I never got to London to see the damage, either, you know. Never took a pass to London. Like I said, we were stationed outside of London, about thirty miles, at this one estate that we were on. This large estate. We was --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: These people --

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: -- creeper -- huh?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were they pretty nice to you, the British people?

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Very nice. Yeah. And down in Cornwall, like I said, we went to town to a dance and struck up acquaintance with a young lady there, you know. And her mother was there at the dance hall. And, then, after the dance I think I went to their house one day and the mother gave me a couple of eggs to take back to camp to fry. They were real nice. Very nice people. Yeah. Yeah, then we were stationed at this -- like I said, this hospital for the prisoners. Then after that we left for France. Off of Southampton. It was interesting on the -- coming over on the Queen Elizabeth, why, we had such a long -- we had about five thousand troops, I guess. But they didn't have so much -- many facilities for feeding. They had two meals a day. You get done with one meal, you go back into the other line. And cold showers or baths. Saltwater baths. Lots of fun. Today I recommend kids to, they should get into the service for a couple of years and enjoy... Maybe they would get to see some of the world a little bit. It's a good experience. I'm glad I got back safe and sound. I'm thankful for that. Of course, my wife was back home praying for me. She would send me lots of letters and we got married after we got back home.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What kind of things would she write to you.

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: Oh, why don't you write? I haven't heard from you for a long time. And they would send over cookies. Oh, the boys would... They still remember it. Oh, we remember Ann's cookies. Her name was Ann. Ah, she was a dear.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you write much back to her?

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: I wrote a lot of these -- what do you call these big --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: E-mail?

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: E-mail stuff. Yeah. I brought her home some perfume, but it stayed in the drawer for a long time. And I brought back some little trinkets from France. That's Mont Saint Michel. I bought her back a nice little sketch, yeah, some kind of a drawing, a pencil drawing or something. In fact, I finally put it up in a frame that I got in my bedroom.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you think about that time do any other vivid memories come to mind?

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: At where?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: During your time overseas?

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: On time overseas? No. No scary moments, I guess. Other than what I've said.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Walking through a mine field sounds plenty scary.

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Oh, then, we were assigned to some volunteer soldiers that would -- they were bored doing nothing; so, they were from North Africa. They had been transferred over to our outfit. And they wanted to do something, have something to do; so, they would go out and look for the mines. And we had to go along with them in case they got blown up. They would find a mine and, then, they would dig underneath and deactivate it. So, yeah, that was kind of scary. Oh, dang. I kind of think I remember a lot of stuff; but, of course, there's some stuff that I have forgotten, I guess.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: And these two fellows from Cape Cod, Art and Charlie, have kept in contact with Christmas cards through the years and, then, finally... Oh, they did stop over. This was Charlie and his wife. And, then, we have another fellow that was Irish. Owen Garrety(phonetic). And he's - - he passed away. But they came out to see me in 1940 -- 1950. They were at a picnic out in Massachusetts and they said, come on, let's go see Eddie Roll. They thought it was a six-hour drive and here they got in the car and they drove and they drove and they drove. And the wife and I went out shopping, grocery shopping. We came home and here's somebody sitting on the lawn. Here was Charlie and his wife, Lucy, and Mary and Owen. So, we fed them, put them to bed; then, the next day they -- they didn't want to -- they didn't want to go anywhere, really. They just wanted to rest. Well, they went to church up to the corner. Then we just sat around and talked; then, they took off again for back home. They were a fun-loving crowd.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I guess.

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: Oh. Art's a funny one, too. That's about all I can say right now.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You think that covers it?

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: Unless you have any questions.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Well, I think you've answered most of my questions.

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: Oh, think so?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You know, I have a little list of questions in my mind and I let you go and usually you'll answer them. You know, I didn't ask you about food, because you already told me about food, you know.

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: I'm a blabbermouth. I don't talk, really, too much, but...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Well, you know, one question, I guess, I didn't ask is what was your reunion with your wife like when you finally got back?

sp.speaker: Edward Roll
sp.p: Well, that was cute. She came down to the terminal. I left Camp Attebury in the morning, I guess. And I got into Cleveland at Terminal Tower, you know. They used to have the trains there yet. And it was about, I guess, 9:00 o'clock in the morning. And I walked up the stairs and here she was all alone. She didn't want anybody to come down to meet me. She took her -- she asked her father can I -- can I use the car to go downtown and pick up Eddie? That was nice. Such memories such as that are really nice.
